solutions.text: The passage itself concludes that sleep is not a passive interruption but an active part of how new memories become stable, and the replay, disruption and sleep deprivation findings all build toward exactly that claim. The claim that disrupting replay impairs performance on every task tested is contradicted by the word 'selectively' and by performance on other tasks remaining intact. The suggestion that awake volunteers remember more because less time has passed ignores the design detail that both groups are tested at the same interval after learning, and the sleepers in fact recall more.

The passage states that grid batteries shift surplus electricity across a few hours and have become cheap, but cannot move a summer surplus to a winter deficit because storing electricity for months remains far too expensive, which is precisely the claim that batteries help over hours but not over whole seasons. The opening sentence says renewable output follows the weather rather than demand, so the claim that it follows demand reverses the passage. Despite cheap batteries, the final sentence still lists long duration storage, flexible demand, overbuilt generation and backup plants as necessary, so none of those can be dropped.

The decisive fact: the 1906 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine was shared by Camillo Golgi and the Spanish histologist Santiago Ramón y Cajal for their work on the structure of the nervous system, Golgi for the silver staining 'black reaction' that made individual nerve cells visible and Cajal for using it to establish the neuron doctrine. Pavlov (1904), von Behring (1901) and Koch (1905) won in adjacent years for different work, and Sherrington's share came much later, in 1932.

The decisive fact: at the Milano Cortina 2026 Winter Games Norway finished at the top of the final medal table with a record 18 gold medals and 41 medals in total, extending its run of leading the Winter Games tables from 2018 and 2022. The United States (33 medals) and the Netherlands followed, and the host nation Italy, despite exceeding its own goals, did not lead the table.

Givens: some buses in the city fleet are electric; every electric vehicle is exempt from the congestion charge; no exempt vehicle may use the toll road.
Take the electric buses: being electric vehicles, each of them is exempt from the congestion charge.
Each of those exempt buses is therefore barred from the toll road.
The fleet does contain such buses, so at least some buses in the city fleet may not use the toll road.
That chain uses only the given premises, so this conclusion must be true.
Classic slip: the reversal that every exempt vehicle is electric does not follow from an all-to-some premise, and nothing constrains the non electric buses, so any claim about all buses or about the non electric ones overreaches.

Givens: five runners, places 1 to 5, no ties; Lena third; Carmen immediately behind Lena; Devi behind Carmen; Bruno not first.
Carmen immediately behind third place puts Carmen fourth.
The only place behind fourth is fifth, so Devi is fifth.
Places 1 and 2 are left for Aisha and Bruno.
Bruno did not finish first, so Aisha is first and Bruno is second.
The order Aisha, Bruno, Lena, Carmen, Devi fits every clue and is the only possible one, so Bruno finished second.
Classic slip: the claim that Devi finished fourth ignores that fourth is already occupied by Carmen, who finished immediately behind Lena.

Givens: 100 children, each does at least one activity; 55 swim, 50 sail, 45 archery; 25 swim and sail, 20 swim and archery, 15 sail and archery; 10 do all three.
Each pair figure still contains the 10 children who do all three, so exactly-two counts equal the pair figures minus 10.
Swim and sail only: 25 − 10 = 15.
Swim and archery only: 20 − 10 = 10.
Sail and archery only: 15 − 10 = 5.
Exactly two activities: 15 + 10 + 5 = 30.
Check: the only-one regions come to 20, 20 and 20 (for swimming 55 − 25 − 20 + 10 = 20), and 20 + 20 + 20 + 15 + 10 + 5 + 10 = 100, matching the camp.
Classic slip: the value 40 counts children doing at least two activities, because it leaves the 10 triple-overlap children inside every pair total.

Givens: 1 April 2026 was a Wednesday; Mondays recur every 7 days.
Count forward from Wednesday 1 April: 2 April Thursday, 3 April Friday, 4 April Saturday, 5 April Sunday, 6 April Monday.
So the first Monday is 6 April.
Add 7 days for each later Monday: 6 + 7 = 13 April, then 13 + 7 = 20 April, then 20 + 7 = 27 April.
The Mondays of April 2026 are therefore 6, 13, 20 and 27 April, and the second of them is 13 April.
Classic slip: 6 April is only the first Monday, and 12 April is a Sunday, one day before the second Monday.

Givens: the net is a column of four squares numbered 5, 1, 3, 6 from top to bottom, with square 2 attached to the left edge of square 1 and square 4 to its right edge.
The column of four folds into a band that wraps around four faces of the cube.
In a four-square band, squares two positions apart end up opposite, so 5 opposes 3 and 1 opposes 6.
The two side squares 2 and 4 fold up on either side of face 1 and end up opposite each other.
So the face opposite the face numbered 1 carries the number 6.
Classic slip: 2, 3, 4 and 5 are the labels of faces adjacent to face 1 in the folded cube, and adjacent faces cannot be opposite.

Step 1: helicase unwinds the parental double helix, primase lays the short RNA primers, DNA polymerase can only extend an existing primer (it cannot start a chain), and ligase seals the gaps between adjacent fragments. Step 2: because the two template strands are antiparallel, only one new strand can be made continuously in the direction of fork opening, from a single primer; the other is built in short fragments, each started by its own primer. The claim that helicase makes the primers gives that job to the wrong enzyme (it belongs to primase), and the claim that the leading strand needs a new primer for every fragment describes the lagging strand instead.

RNA polymerase binds the promoter sequence (the terminator instead signals where transcription stops) and initiates RNA synthesis without any primer, unlike DNA polymerase, while reading one DNA strand as the template. The new RNA grows in the 5' to 3' direction, so the claim that synthesis runs 3' to 5' reverses the actual direction. The poly-A tail is not transcribed from the gene; it is added enzymatically to the 3' end of the finished pre-mRNA in the nucleus.

During elongation a tRNA carrying the next amino acid enters at the A (aminoacyl) site of the ribosome and its anticodon base pairs with the mRNA codon exposed there; peptidyl transferase then transfers the growing chain onto it, and tRNAs step through the P (peptidyl) site and leave by the E (exit) site. The initiator tRNA starts in the P site, not the A site, peptide bonds form at the peptidyl transferase centre of the large subunit rather than at the exit site, and the growing chain rides on the P site tRNA, not on newly entering ones. Bacteria can translate an mRNA while it is still being transcribed, but eukaryotes cannot, since their transcription happens in the nucleus and translation in the cytoplasm.

Step 1: mutation 1 changes codon 2 from GCA to GCC, and both codons specify alanine, so it is silent. Step 2: mutation 2 inserts one base after codon 2, shifting the reading frame: the tail UAC GGU UAA now regroups as GUA, CGG, UUA, which encode valine, arginine and leucine in place of tyrosine, glycine and the stop signal, so every amino acid from position 3 changes and translation runs past the old stop. The suggestion that an insertion adds exactly one amino acid or changes only one position confuses an insertion with a substitution; only inserting or deleting a multiple of three bases would leave the downstream reading frame intact.

The testcross parent aabbcc can contribute only recessive alleles, so at each locus the cross is effectively Aa × aa, giving heterozygous offspring with probability 1/2 and homozygous recessive offspring with probability 1/2. The three genes assort independently, so the probabilities multiply: 1/2 × 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/8. The ratio 3/4 belongs to a heterozygote self cross, where three of four offspring show the dominant phenotype, and has no place in a testcross.

An affected child from two unaffected parents proves that both parents are carriers, so each pregnancy gives 1/4 AA, 1/2 Aa and 1/4 aa. Conditioning on the child being healthy removes only the aa class, leaving one AA to two Aa among unaffected offspring, so the probability that the healthy child is a carrier is 2/3. The unconditional carrier risk for any child of carrier parents is 1/2, which ignores the given information that this particular child is unaffected.

The woman's father passed his only X chromosome, which carried the allele, to all his daughters, so she is certainly a carrier; her unaffected husband passes a normal X to every child. The probability that the first child is a daughter is 1/2, and a daughter of a carrier mother has a 1/2 chance of receiving the mother's mutant X, giving 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4. Stopping at 1/2 forgets to include the chance that the child is a girl at all.

Since 13 = 4 + 9, the largest recombination frequency is the sum of the other two, which is the signature of the middle gene lying between the outer two: the map order is a, then b 4 units away, then c a further 9 units away. If a or c were the middle gene, the largest distance would have to equal the difference of the other two, not the sum. Genes on three different chromosomes would assort independently and give pairwise recombination frequencies near 50 percent, not 4, 9 and 13 percent.

Anaphase of mitosis begins when the sister chromatids separate at their centromeres and are pulled toward opposite spindle poles. The separation of homologous chromosome pairs happens in anaphase I of meiosis, not mitosis; alignment at the cell's equator is metaphase; breakdown of the nuclear envelope belongs to prophase; and re-formation of nuclear envelopes around each chromosome group is telophase.

Step 1: nondisjunction of sister chromatids in meiosis II sends both copies of chromosome 21 into one egg (24 chromosomes) and none into the other, while meiosis I has already halved the set normally. Step 2: fertilisation of the egg carrying both copies by a normal sperm (23 chromosomes) gives 24 + 23 = 47 chromosomes, with three copies of chromosome 21, which is trisomy 21, Down syndrome. All other chromosomes are present in the usual two copies, so totals of 45, 46 or 69 are impossible, and the extra chromosome is chromosome 21, not a sex chromosome.

The dark form arises by random mutation before the environment changes; once soot darkened the trunks, birds caught the more visible light moths, so dark moths survived and reproduced more successfully and passed on their alleles, which is natural selection acting on pre-existing variation. The alternative routes fail: individual moths cannot acquire heritable darkening during their own lifetimes, soot does not chemically rewrite genes, moths cannot produce dark offspring 'in order to' match a background, and the passage states that light moths greatly outnumbered dark ones before the trees darkened.

The tetraploid plants arose within the same meadow as the diploids, so there is no geographic barrier, which rules out any allopatric account and the claim that a physical barrier is always required. Because tetraploid × diploid crosses produce seeds that die, the polyploids are reproductively isolated, so a new lineage has formed in sympatry, and polyploidy is the classic one step route to speciation in plants. Sharing a meadow does not by itself make one biological species: the species criterion is interbreeding, not geography, and a change in chromosome number clearly can create a new species here.

The oxygen released in photosynthesis comes from the splitting (photolysis) of water at photosystem II in the thylakoid membranes: the water's electrons replace those lost by the photosystem and its oxygen atoms are released as O₂. Electrons from water pass to photosystem II first, not directly to photosystem I; the splitting happens in the thylakoid membrane, not in the stroma, where the Calvin cycle instead fixes CO₂; and ATP is made afterwards by chemiosmosis, not directly by the splitting step. The claim that the released oxygen comes from carbon dioxide has the source backwards.

Xylem, made of dead hollow vessels, carries water and dissolved mineral ions upward from the roots, driven mainly by transpiration pull, while phloem's living sieve tubes carry sucrose from source tissues such as mature leaves to sink tissues such as roots, fruits and buds, and the phloem flow can run upward or downward. Swapping the two cargoes inverts the roles of the tissues, transpiration pull does not move phloem contents, and mature xylem is dead rather than living and actively pumping. The claim that sugars move only downward fails because sinks such as growing shoots sit above the leaves.

Step 1: the impulse from the sinoatrial node spreads across the atria, which contract first. Step 2: conduction is delayed briefly at the atrioventricular node before the impulse continues through the bundle of His and the Purkinje fibres to the ventricles. Step 3: this electrical delay, not the time blood takes to flow and not a difference in muscle contraction speed, lets the atria finish emptying before ventricular contraction begins. There is only one impulse initiating each beat, and the ventricles never contract first in a healthy heart.

Hydrostatic blood pressure in the glomerular capillaries forces water and small solutes (glucose, urea, ions, amino acids) through the filtration barrier into Bowman's capsule, while plasma proteins and blood cells are too large to cross and remain in the blood. Glucose enters the filtrate by filtration and is then reabsorbed in the proximal convoluted tubule; it is not actively secreted into the filtrate, and water leaves the capillaries under pressure rather than by active transport. The idea that proteins are filtered freely and reclaimed later describes a leakiness a healthy glomerulus does not have, and blood cells never normally reach the filtrate.

Action potentials are all or none events: once threshold is reached, every impulse has the same fixed amplitude, and stimulus strength is encoded as firing frequency, so a stronger stimulus produces more impulses per second, never larger ones. Subthreshold stimuli produce no action potential at all, rather than small slow ones. The refractory period guarantees one way propagation by preventing immediate re-excitation behind the impulse, and repolarisation carries the membrane potential back down toward the negative resting value, not above the depolarisation peak.

The hypothalamus secretes CRH, the anterior pituitary responds by releasing ACTH into the bloodstream, and ACTH stimulates the adrenal cortex to secrete cortisol; rising cortisol then inhibits CRH and ACTH release, a negative feedback loop. Cortisol comes from the cortex, not the medulla, which secretes adrenaline under direct nerve control; a fall in cortisol would release the brake and increase, not decrease, ACTH output; and ACTH is a blood borne hormone, not a signal travelling down nerve fibres. The loop is negative, not positive, feedback.

B lymphocytes mature in the bone marrow and, when activated, differentiate into plasma cells that secrete antibodies; T lymphocytes mature in the thymus, and cytotoxic T cells kill infected host cells by direct contact. Antibody secretion is the job of B cells, not T cells; phagocytosis of bacteria belongs to macrophages and neutrophils, not cytotoxic T cells; and only the T cells complete their maturation in the thymus, so placing B cell maturation there misassigns the site.

Microtubules are hollow polymers of the protein tubulin that build the mitotic spindle and form the axoneme at the core of cilia and flagella. The claim that the contractile ring dividing an animal cell at cytokinesis is made of microtubules, and the claim that actin microfilaments form the spindle fibres, each swap the real roles of microtubules and actin: the ring is actin, the spindle is tubulin. Calling microtubules permanently fixed structures also contradicts their constant dynamic assembly and disassembly.

Apoptosis is programmed cell death: internal or external signals activate regulated pathways that fragment the DNA, shrink the cell and package it into membrane bound fragments that neighbouring cells engulf, so no digestive enzymes spill into the tissue and inflammation is avoided. It is essential in healthy development, for instance in removing the webbing between developing fingers. Uncontrolled death after injury with enzyme release and inflammation describes necrosis, and apoptosis is commonly triggered by signals arising within the cell, not only by external toxins.

Primary structure is the linear sequence of amino acids joined by covalent peptide bonds. Hydrogen bonding between backbone atoms defines secondary structure (alpha helices and beta sheets), disulfide bridges between cysteines stabilise the tertiary fold rather than the secondary structure, and the assembly of several separate polypeptide chains into one functional unit is quaternary, not tertiary, structure. Calling the local coiling into alpha helices quaternary structure assigns a secondary feature to the wrong level.

Falling body temperature is detected and the hypothalamus, the thermoregulatory centre, mounts heat generating and heat conserving responses: shivering, the involuntary rapid contraction of skeletal muscle whose metabolism releases heat, together with vasoconstriction of skin vessels and reduced sweating, all part of a negative feedback loop restoring core temperature. Shivering is not a voluntary choice, skin vessels constrict rather than widen in the cold, and increased sweating is the cooling response to heat, not to cold.

Given: n = 0.25 mol of CuSO₄; atomic masses Cu = 64, S = 32, O = 16 g/mol.
Relationship: the molar mass M is the sum of the atomic masses in the formula, and mass m = n × M.
M(CuSO₄) = 64 + 32 + (4 × 16) = 64 + 32 + 64 = 160 g/mol.
Substitute: m = 0.25 mol × 160 g/mol.
0.25 × 160 = 40, so m = 40 g.
Result: 40 g.
Classic slip: 160 g is the mass of a whole mole, and 640 g comes from dividing 160 by 0.25 instead of multiplying.

Given: 28 g of N₂ (M = 28 g/mol), 9.0 g of H₂ (M = 2.0 g/mol), N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃, M(NH₃) = 17 g/mol.
Relationship: n = m/M; the equation ratio is 1 mol N₂ : 3 mol H₂ : 2 mol NH₃, so compare available moles to find the limiting reagent.
n(N₂) = 28/28 = 1.0 mol.
n(H₂) = 9.0/2.0 = 4.5 mol.
H₂ needed for all the N₂: 3 × 1.0 = 3.0 mol; 4.5 mol are available, so H₂ is in excess and N₂ is limiting.
NH₃ produced: 2 × 1.0 = 2.0 mol.
m(NH₃) = 2.0 × 17 = 34 g.
Result: 34 g.
Classic slip: 51 g treats hydrogen as limiting and converts all of it (4.5 × 2/3 = 3.0 mol NH₃, then 3.0 × 17 = 51 g), ignoring that the nitrogen runs out first.

Given: 50.0% sulfur and 50.0% oxygen by mass; S = 32 g/mol, O = 16 g/mol.
Relationship: take a 100 g sample, convert each mass to moles with n = m/M, then divide both mole numbers by the smaller.
n(S) = 50.0/32 = 1.56 mol.
n(O) = 50.0/16 = 3.13 mol.
Divide by the smaller: 1.56/1.56 = 1.0 for S.
3.13/1.56 ≈ 2.0 for O.
Ratio S : O ≈ 1 : 2, so the empirical formula is SO₂.
Result: SO₂.
Classic slip: the formula SO assumes equal masses mean equal moles, but an oxygen atom is only half the mass of a sulfur atom, so equal masses hold twice as many moles of O.

Given: m = 5.85 g of NaCl, M = 58.5 g/mol, final volume V = 500 cm³.
Relationship: n = m/M, then concentration c = n/V with V converted to dm³ (1000 cm³ = 1 dm³).
n(NaCl) = 5.85/58.5 = 0.10 mol.
V = 500/1000 = 0.500 dm³.
Substitute: c = 0.10/0.500 = 0.20 mol/dm³.
Result: 0.20 mol/dm³.
Classic slip: 0.10 mol/dm³ merely relabels the mole number as a concentration, ignoring that the salt was made up to half a cubic decimetre.

Given: [KOH] = 1.0 × 10⁻⁴ mol/dm³, KOH dissociates completely, Kw = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ at 25 °C.
Relationship: a fully dissociated strong base gives [OH⁻] equal to its concentration; pOH = −log₁₀[OH⁻]; pH + pOH = 14 at 25 °C.
[OH⁻] = 1.0 × 10⁻⁴ mol/dm³, so pOH = 4.
Substitute: pH = 14 − 4 = 10.
Result: pH 10.
Classic slip: the value 4 is the pOH mislabelled as pH; a solution of a strong base can be neither acidic nor exactly neutral.

At the equivalence point the moles of H⁺ and OH⁻ have reacted exactly, and since NaCl is the salt of a strong acid and a strong base it does not hydrolyse, leaving the solution neutral at pH 7 at 25 °C. Equivalence means equal moles, not equal masses, of acid and base, and the indicator's colour change defines the endpoint, a related but distinct point. The claim that every equivalence point sits at pH 7 fails for weak acid or weak base systems: titrating a weak acid with NaOH gives an alkaline equivalence point because the conjugate base hydrolyses.

Given: unbalanced MnO₄⁻ + C₂O₄²⁻ + H⁺ → Mn²⁺ + CO₂ + H₂O in acidic solution.
Relationship: balance with half equations, then equalise the electrons lost and gained.
Reduction: MnO₄⁻ + 8H⁺ + 5e⁻ → Mn²⁺ + 4H₂O, since Mn falls from +7 to +2 (5 electrons gained) and 4 oxygen atoms need 4 H₂O, whose 8 H come from 8 H⁺.
Oxidation: C₂O₄²⁻ → 2CO₂ + 2e⁻, since each C rises from +3 to +4, so 2 electrons are lost per ion.
Equalise electrons: the lowest common multiple of 5 and 2 is 10, so multiply the reduction by 2 (2 × 5 = 10 electrons) and the oxidation by 5 (5 × 2 = 10 electrons).
Add: 2MnO₄⁻ + 5C₂O₄²⁻ + 16H⁺ → 2Mn²⁺ + 10CO₂ + 8H₂O; the 16 H⁺ come from 2 × 8 and supply the 8 × 2 = 16 H in 8 H₂O.
Result: the coefficient of H⁺ is 16.
Classic slip: 8 is the H⁺ count of one permanganate half equation, forgetting that two of them must be multiplied in to match the 10 electrons from five oxalate ions.

Boron has three valence electrons and forms three bonds in BF₃, leaving only six electrons in its valence shell; the molecule is electron deficient and readily accepts a lone pair, which is exactly the behaviour of a Lewis acid. PCl₅ (10 electrons around phosphorus) and SF₆ (12 around sulfur) do exist, because period 3 atoms can expand their octets, so exceeding the octet cannot forbid their existence. Nitrogen in NH₃ holds eight valence electrons (three bonding pairs plus a lone pair), not ten, and phosphorus in PCl₅ has ten electrons around it, not an octet's eight.

Halogens react as oxidising agents by gaining one electron; descending the group, the atomic radius and inner shell shielding increase, so the attraction for an added electron weakens and reactivity falls from fluorine to iodine. Consequently the more reactive halogen always displaces the less reactive one from its salts: chlorine displaces bromine from bromide solutions, and bromine cannot displace chlorine from potassium chloride. Boiling points rise down the group (chlorine is a gas, bromine a liquid, iodine a solid), and halogens are poor electrical conductors.

Given: standard enthalpies of formation in kJ/mol: CH₄ = −75, CO₂ = −394, H₂O(l) = −286, O₂ = 0; equation CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O.
Relationship: ΔH = ΣΔHf(products) − ΣΔHf(reactants).
Substitute: ΔH = [(−394) + 2 × (−286)] − [(−75) + 0].
Water term: 2 × (−286) = −572.
Products: −394 + (−572) = −966.
Reactants: −75 + 0 = −75.
ΔH = −966 − (−75) = −966 + 75 = −891 kJ/mol.
Result: −891 kJ/mol.
Classic slip: −605 kJ/mol drops the factor of 2 on the water term (−394 − 286 + 75), and the positive options additionally reverse the products minus reactants order; a combustion cannot be endothermic.

Given: H₂ + I₂ ⇌ 2HI; at equilibrium [H₂] = 0.20 mol/dm³, [I₂] = 0.30 mol/dm³, [HI] = 0.60 mol/dm³.
Relationship: Kc = [HI]² / ([H₂] × [I₂]); the coefficient 2 before HI squares its concentration.
Substitute: Kc = (0.60)² / (0.20 × 0.30).
Numerator: 0.60 × 0.60 = 0.36.
Denominator: 0.20 × 0.30 = 0.060.
Kc = 0.36/0.060 = 6.0.
Result: Kc = 6.0, with no units because the concentration powers cancel.
Classic slip: the value 10 leaves [HI] unsquared (0.60/0.060 = 10), and about 0.17 inverts the whole fraction.

Given: experiment 1: [A] = 0.10 mol/dm³, [B] = 0.10 mol/dm³, rate = 0.0020 mol/(dm³ s); experiment 2: [A] = 0.20, [B] = 0.10, rate = 0.0040; experiment 3: [A] = 0.10, [B] = 0.20, rate = 0.0080.
Relationship: rate = k[A]^m[B]^n; compare pairs of experiments that change only one concentration.
Experiments 1 to 2: [B] is fixed, [A] doubles from 0.10 to 0.20 and the rate doubles from 0.0020 to 0.0040, so m = 1.
Experiments 1 to 3: [A] is fixed, [B] doubles from 0.10 to 0.20 and the rate quadruples from 0.0020 to 0.0080, so n = 2 (doubling twice: 0.0020 → 0.0040 → 0.0080).
Rate law: rate = k[A][B]², overall order 1 + 2 = 3.
Result: rate = k[A][B]².
Classic slip: rate = k[A][B] predicts only a doubling of rate between experiments 1 and 3, not the observed quadrupling.

Givens: a five-carbon chain with one methyl group on carbon 2 and one on carbon 4.
Longest continuous chain: 5 carbons, so the parent alkane is pentane; no path through 6 carbons exists, so any hexane-based name is impossible.
Two identical substituents: the prefix is dimethyl.
Numbering: the substitution pattern is symmetric, so from either end of the chain the methyl groups fall on carbons 2 and 4.
Lowest-locant rule: 2 and 4 are already the lowest possible positions, giving 2,4-dimethylpentane.
Classic slip: the name 3,5-dimethylpentane uses locants that are never acceptable, because the chain must always be numbered from the end that gives the lowest positions.

Sunlight (ultraviolet) splits Cl₂ into chlorine radicals; a chlorine radical abstracts a hydrogen atom from methane to give HCl and a methyl radical, which then reacts with another Cl₂ molecule to form CH₃Cl and regenerate a chlorine radical. One hydrogen of methane is replaced by chlorine with the carbon skeleton unchanged, which is the definition of free radical substitution. It is not electrophilic addition (methane has no double bond to add across), not nucleophilic substitution (no nucleophile attacks a carbon centre), and not an elimination.

Givens: iron has atomic number 26, so a neutral atom holds 26 electrons; Fe²⁺ has lost 2 and holds 24.
Fill the neutral atom in aufbau order: 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s2 3d6, with 4s filling before 3d.
Count check: 2 + 2 + 6 + 2 + 6 + 2 + 6 = 26 electrons.
Ionisation removes the highest-energy electrons first, which are the two 4s electrons, not any 3d electrons.
Remove the 4s pair: 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 3d6, leaving 24 electrons.
Result: the configuration of Fe²⁺ is 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 3d6.
Classic slip: the arrangement 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 3d4 4s2 keeps the 4s pair and strips 3d electrons instead, reversing the true order in which electrons leave on ionisation.

Given: log₂x + log₂(x − 6) = 4.
Relationship: log₂a + log₂b = log₂(ab); log₂y = 4 means y = 2⁴; logarithms demand positive arguments, so x > 0 and x − 6 > 0, that is x > 6.
Combine: log₂(x(x − 6)) = 4, so x(x − 6) = 2⁴ = 16.
Rearrange: x² − 6x − 16 = 0.
Factorise: (x − 8)(x + 2) = 0, so x = 8 or x = −2.
Apply the domain x > 6: x = −2 is rejected, so x = 8.
Check: log₂8 + log₂(8 − 6) = 3 + 1 = 4.
Result: x = 8 only.
Classic slip: keeping x = −2 ignores the domain, since there x − 6 = −8 and the logarithm of a negative number does not exist.

Given: a committee of 3 chosen from 4 chemists and 6 physicists, so 10 people in all; wanted: exactly one chemist.
Relationship: probability = favourable committees ÷ total committees, with C(n,r) = n!/(r!(n − r)!).
Total committees: C(10,3) = (10 × 9 × 8)/(3 × 2 × 1) = 720/6 = 120.
Favourable: the one chemist can be picked in C(4,1) = 4 ways.
The two physicists can be picked in C(6,2) = (6 × 5)/2 = 15 ways.
Favourable committees: 4 × 15 = 60.
Substitute: P = 60/120 = 1/2.
Result: 1/2.
Classic slip: quoting the raw count 60 without dividing by the 120 possible committees, or mixing ordered and unordered counts, gives the other fractions.

Given: f(x) = x² − 4x; wanted: f(x + 3) − 2.
Relationship: replace every x by x + 3, expand, then subtract 2.
Substitute: f(x + 3) = (x + 3)² − 4(x + 3).
Square: (x + 3)² = x² + 6x + 9.
Expand: 4(x + 3) = 4x + 12, so −4(x + 3) = −4x − 12.
Combine: x² + 6x + 9 − 4x − 12 = x² + 2x − 3.
Subtract 2: x² + 2x − 3 − 2 = x² + 2x − 5.
Result: x² + 2x − 5.
Classic slip: x² − 10x + 19 results from shifting the wrong way, substituting x − 3 instead of x + 3.

Given: cos(2x) = 1/2 with 0 ≤ x ≤ 2π, so t = 2x runs over 0 ≤ t ≤ 4π, two full turns.
Relationship: within one turn of 2π, cos t = 1/2 at t = π/3 and t = 5π/3; each further turn adds 2π.
First turn: t = π/3 and t = 5π/3.
Second turn: t = π/3 + 2π = 7π/3 and t = 5π/3 + 2π = 11π/3.
Divide by 2: x = π/6, 5π/6, 7π/6, 11π/6, all inside the interval.
Result: 4 solutions.
Classic slip: the answer 2 searches only one period of cosine, forgetting that doubling the angle doubles the range to be searched.

Given: the inequality (x + 1)/(x − 2) ≥ 0.
Relationship: a quotient is ≥ 0 when numerator and denominator share a sign or the numerator is 0; it is undefined where the denominator is 0.
Boundary points: numerator 0 at x = −1 (allowed, since 0 ≥ 0); denominator 0 at x = 2 (excluded).
Sign test: for x < −1 both parts are negative, so the quotient is positive; for −1 < x < 2 the signs differ, so it is negative; for x > 2 both parts are positive.
Collect the positive-or-zero regions: x ≤ −1 or x > 2.
Result: x ≤ −1 or x > 2.
Classic slip: writing x ≥ 2 includes x = 2, where the denominator vanishes and the fraction has no value.

Given: a square inscribed in a circle of radius r = 6 cm.
Relationship: an inscribed square has each diagonal equal to the diameter, d = 2r, and the area of a square from its diagonal is A = d²/2.
Substitute: d = 2 × 6 = 12 cm.
A = 12²/2 = 144/2 = 72 cm².
Result: 72 cm².
Classic slip: 36 cm² treats the 6 cm radius as the side length, but a square of side 6 has a diagonal of about 8.5 cm and would not even touch a circle of radius 6.

Given: arithmetic sequence with 3rd term 11 and 8th term 31.
Relationship: nth term = a + (n − 1)d; sum of the first n terms S = (n/2)(2a + (n − 1)d).
Common difference: d = (31 − 11)/(8 − 3) = 20/5 = 4.
First term: a = 11 − (3 − 1) × 4 = 11 − 8 = 3.
Substitute: S₁₀ = (10/2) × (2 × 3 + 9 × 4).
Inner terms: 2 × 3 = 6 and 9 × 4 = 36, so 2a + 9d = 6 + 36 = 42.
S₁₀ = 5 × 42 = 210.
Result: 210.
Classic slip: 290 treats the 3rd term as the first term (a = 11 gives 5 × (22 + 36) = 290), forgetting to step back two places to the true first term.

Given: launch speed 20 m/s at 30° above the horizontal; g = 10 m/s²; sin 30° = 0.5.
Relationship: only the vertical component climbs: v0y = v × sin 30°; at the highest point the vertical velocity is momentarily 0, and v² = u² − 2gh then gives h = v0y²/(2g).
Vertical component: v0y = 20 × 0.5 = 10 m/s.
Substitute: h = 10²/(2 × 10) = 100/20 = 5 m.
Result: 5 m.
Classic slip: 20 m squares the full launch speed of 20 m/s instead of its vertical component of 10 m/s.

Given: m = 4.0 kg, KE = 200 J.
Relationship: KE = ½mv², so v² = 2 × KE/m and v = √(2 × KE/m).
Substitute: 200 = ½ × 4.0 × v².
½ × 4.0 = 2.0, so v² = 200/2.0 = 100 m²/s².
v = √100 = 10 m/s.
Result: 10 m/s.
Classic slip: 5 m/s comes from multiplying by ½ instead of dividing by it (v² = (0.5 × 200)/4 = 25), and 100 m/s forgets the square root altogether (2 × 200/4 = 100).

Given: m₁ = 2.0 kg moving at 6.0 m/s; m₂ = 4.0 kg at rest; head-on perfectly elastic collision on a frictionless track.
Relationship: momentum is conserved, and in an elastic collision the relative speed of separation equals the relative speed of approach.
Momentum: 2.0 × 6.0 = 2.0v₁ + 4.0v₂, so 12 = 2.0v₁ + 4.0v₂.
Relative speed: v₂ − v₁ = 6.0, so v₁ = v₂ − 6.0.
Substitute: 12 = 2.0(v₂ − 6.0) + 4.0v₂ = 2.0v₂ − 12 + 4.0v₂ = 6.0v₂ − 12.
Solve: 6.0v₂ = 24, so v₂ = 4.0 m/s (and v₁ = −2.0 m/s, the light trolley rebounds).
Energy check: before, ½ × 2.0 × 6.0² = 36 J; after, ½ × 2.0 × 2.0² + ½ × 4.0 × 4.0² = 4 + 32 = 36 J.
Result: the 4.0 kg trolley moves off at 4 m/s.
Classic slip: 6 m/s for the heavy trolley would force the light one backwards at 6 m/s and give 36 + 72 = 108 J, tripling the kinetic energy that was available.

Given: weight W = 50 N; object density 2500 kg/m³; water density 1000 kg/m³; g = 10 m/s²; object fully submerged and held at rest.
Relationship: at rest the forces balance, T + U = W, where the upthrust U = ρ_water × g × V and V = m/ρ_object with m = W/g.
Mass: m = 50/10 = 5 kg.
Volume: V = 5/2500 = 0.002 m³.
Upthrust: U = 1000 × 10 × 0.002 = 20 N.
Tension: T = W − U = 50 − 20 = 30 N.
Result: 30 N.
Classic slip: 50 N ignores buoyancy altogether, and 70 N adds the upthrust instead of subtracting it, the wrong sign for a force that pushes upward.

Given: m = 0.30 kg of oil, c = 2000 J/(kg K), heated from 20 °C to 70 °C.
Relationship: Q = m × c × ΔT, with ΔT the temperature rise (a rise of 50 °C equals 50 K).
ΔT = 70 − 20 = 50 K.
Substitute: Q = 0.30 × 2000 × 50.
0.30 × 2000 = 600, then 600 × 50 = 30 000 J.
Q = 30 000 J = 30 kJ.
Result: 30 kJ.
Classic slip: 15 kJ uses half the temperature rise (0.30 × 2000 × 25), and 3.0 kJ is out by a factor of ten through a decimal slip in the mass or the rise.

Given: V = 12 V across a single R = 8 Ω resistor, negligible internal resistance.
Relationship: P = V²/R; equivalently I = V/R then P = V × I.
Substitute: P = 12²/8 = 144/8 = 18 W.
Cross-check by current: I = 12/8 = 1.5 A, then P = 12 × 1.5 = 18 W.
Result: 18 W.
Classic slip: 144 W stops at V² without dividing by the resistance, 96 W multiplies V by R, and 1.5 is the current in amperes rather than a power.
